text: Bradley is a 62-year-old White man with history of lung cancer who presents with sudden onset of back pain. Bradley states that the pain began suddenly while he was cooking breakfast. Bradley asserts that the pain is worst in his lower back and radiates down the front of his thighs. Bradley has tried taking some ibuprofen and acetaminophen, but he has had no relief. On physical exam, you find that he is tender to palpation of the mid-lumbar spine and that he has pain limited-movement of his hip flexors. MRI of the lumbar spine reveals a pathologic fracture of his L3 vertebral body, canal and neuroforaminal stenosis, and evidence of metastatic disease.

Brett is a 24-year-old White man with neurofibromatosis who presents with progressive pelvic and right leg pain. Brett describes two days of increasing pain in his groin with radiation down his right leg. The pain is severe and he has tried ibuprofen and acetaminophen, but he says these have not helped. The pain was beginning to affect his ability to walk, so he decided to come to the emergency room. Brett's physical exam is remarkable for severe pain limitation on right hip flexion, and he describes diffuse dysesthesias while you palpate his leg. CT and MRI of the pelvis reveal a large mass in the region of his right lumbosacral plexus, and preliminary read is consistent with a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

Scott is a 75-year-old White man with multiple myeloma who presents with new diffuse midline back pain. Scott had been doing well until this morning, when he experienced a sudden spike of sharp pain in his back. Scott was escorted by a family member to the hospital. In the emergency room, he is moaning in agony and complaining about pain in his back. Scott refuses to participate in the physical exam until his pain controlled, but you observe that he is moving all extremities well. You convince Scott to cooperate with a CT scan, which reveals innumerable lytic lesions and multiple pathologic fractures throughout his spine consistent with recurrent myeloma.

Kurt is a 52-year-old White man with hepatitis C and cirrhosis who presents with new abdominal pain. Kurt was preparing breakfast when he had sudden onset of sharp pain in his right upper abdomen. Kurt denies any nausea or vomiting, but he feels the pain worse with inspiration and is in severe discomfort. On physical examination, you find that he is guarding his abdomen, which is tender to palpation of his right upper quadrant. CT of the abdomen reveals a hepatic mass with evidence of hemorrhage.

Todd is a 63-year-old White man with history of renal cell carcinoma who presents with acute neck pain. Todd says he has had neck discomfort for several weeks, but It suddenly became worse today. Todd endorses severe pain that is worse with flexion and extension of his neck, and he has had no relief with ibuprofen. During his physical examination, he does not have any neurological deficits, but you note tenderness to palpation of the back of his neck.

Chad is a 63-year-old White man with history of renal cell carcinoma who presents with acute neck and arm pain. Chad says he has had neck discomfort for several weeks, but It suddenly became worse this morning, when he had an episode of electrical pain shooting down his arms and back . Chad endorses severe pain that is worse with flexion and extension of his neck and denies any recent trauma. In attempts to control the pain he has tried ibuprofen and acetaminophen with no relief. On physical examination, you note that he is very tender to palpation of his cervical spine and that flexion of the neck elicits severe shooting pains down his spine. MRI of the cervical spine shows multifocal lesions throughout his cervical spine, with pathologic fracture of C4 and canal stenosis.

Matthew is a 66-year-old White man with history of hepatocellular carcinoma who presents with acute mid back pain. Matthew states that the pain started after he attempted lifting a heavy piece of furniture yesterday. Since onset of the pain, he also noticed that maintaining his balance has been more difficult and that he has been stumbling more. Matthew also endorses that the pain is even more severe when he attempts to bend or stretch his back. When you examine Matthew, you notice that he is tender to palpation in the mid-thoracic spine, and that he has a positive Romberg sign. You obtain MRI of the thoracic spine, which reveals diffuse osseous metastatic lesions with a severe pathologic fracture at T6.

Dustin is a 50-year-old White man presenting with severe left posterior thigh pain. Dustin states that he has had discomfort in his left thigh for several weeks, but this progressed into frank pain two days ago. Dustin tried taking ibuprofen and acetaminophen but he had no relief from the pain. On physical examination, you discover that he has diminished sensation in several dermatomes spanning his left leg. You obtain an MRI of the lumbosacral spine and discover a large parasacral mass extending toward his pelvic floor.

Shane is a 47-year-old White man with history of Von Hippel Lindau disease who presents with 3 days of progressive shoulder pain and arm paresthesias. Shane reports that he has had long standing shoulder discomfort which transformed into severe pain in the last 72 hours. The pain is associated with intermittent numbness and tingling of both his arms, and he is also having difficulty holding objects. On his physical exam, you detect bilateral diminished sensation in the C5-C6 dermatomes, and weakness of bilateral hand grips. The MRI you obtain shows a cystic lesion involving the spinal cord at levels C5-C7 with an associated syrinx.

Douglas is a 39-year-old White man with lung cancer status-post chemo and radiation therapy who presents with sharp thoracic pain. Douglas states that his pain started 3 days ago and has progressed significantly to the point he can't sleep. Douglas's pain is primarily along the lateral aspects of his and his sternum. Ibuprofen and acetaminophen have provided minimal relief, and he endorses that the pain is sharper and worse during deep inspiration. Douglas's physical exam is remarkable for severe tenderness to palpation of his sternum and lateral rib cage. A CT scan of his chest identifies multiple osseous lesions involving the sternum and bilateral aspects of his rib cage.

Patient B is a 45-year-old with leukemia who presents to the emergency room after completing their final cycle of chemotherapy. Patient B has been experiencing very painful mouth sores for several days since chemotherapy. Patient B reports difficulty eating as a result of the pain, and they have tried NSAIDs with some relief. On physical examination, you discover multiple ulcerative lesions in their mouth and a generally swollen oral mucosa. Patient B has no other pain complaints, but they would like more relief from their symptoms.

Bradley is a 35-year-old White man who presents to your emergency room with complaints of severe abdominal and pelvic pain. Bradley describes the pain as sudden in onset and started shortly after a heavy dinner the night prior. Bradley's pain is worst in the left lower quadrant of his abdomen, and on examination he is tender to palpation of this area with some guarding and rebound tenderness. Bradley is mildly tachycardic, but otherwise has normal vital signs and is afebrile. Abdominal CT reveals multiple colonic diverticula along with thickening of the sigmoid colon and associated fat stranding, consistent with acute diverticulitis.

Brett is a 27-year-old White man presenting with several days of right leg pain since doing a session at the gym. Brett describes the pain as starting in his lower back and radiating down the side and back of his right leg all the way to his foot. Brett describes some paresthesias of his right foot during physical examination, but he has full strength and sensation intact to light touch. An MRI of his lumbar spine reveals a disk herniation at L5-S1 impinging on his right L5 nerve root. Brett's pain is now so severe he is having difficulty ambulating.

Scott is a 17-year-old White man who presents to the emergency room with complaints of severe abdominal pain. Scott is barely able to provide history, but says the pain occurred suddenly after his last meal and has increased in intensity progressively throughout the day. Scott describes the pain as periumbilical, but on physical examination his abdomen is diffusely tender to palpation and the pain is exacerbated by pressing on McBurney’s point. You are unable to obtain additional information because he is in so much pain and is begging for relief. You check his temperature and note a reading of 101.5F.

Kurt is a 40-year-old White man with a history of migraines who presents to the emergency room complaining of a new and severe headache. The pain started 8 hours ago toward a routine shopping trip. Kurt describes it as one of the worst headaches of his life, and states that it was preceded by a visual aura and gradually progressed from unilateral to holo-cranial pain. Kurt also describes photosensitivity and prefers to keep his eyes closed. Kurt has taken ibuprofen, acetaminophen and sumatriptan to no relief. Kurt's history and physical exam is unremarkable. You obtain a head CT, which is negative for intracranial hemorrhage. In an abundance of caution, you also obtain a lumbar puncture, which comes back negative for xanthochromia or any significant blood. The patient is still in agony and now asks if you can give his something to make the pain go away.

Todd is a 62-year-old White man who presents to your emergency room with complaints of chest pain. Todd has poorly controlled hypertension and several coronary artery disease risk factors. Todd's pain is mid-sternal and intermittent, ranging from 4-8/10 and does not correlate with his activity level. Todd denies any radiation of his pain, or any exacerbation with deep inspiration. Todd's EKG shows mild sinus tachycardia and ST segment elevation in the inferior leads. Labs are remarkable for an elevated serum troponin.

Chad is a 44-year-old White man presenting with severe left flank pain. Chad's pain occurs intermittently every and lasts approximately 30 minutes at a time. Chad describes the pain as sometimes radiating to his groin area. Chad endorses generally poor water intake, and a family history of kidney stones. Chad's urinalysis is positive for blood, and a CT scan of his abdomen reveals multiple stones at the left ureteropelvic junction. Just as he is leaving the scanner, he begins to experience another episode of flank pain, and screams in agony.

Matthew is a 32-year-old White man presenting with severe abdominal pain. Matthew's pain began after his last meal, a few hours before his arrival to the emergency room, and reached its full intensity within 30 minutes. You localize his pain on physical exam to the epigastric region, where he is exquisitely tender to palpation. Matthew's labs are remarkable for an elevated serum lipase, and his abdominal CT scan with contrast shows diffuse enlargement of the pancreas and heterogeneous contrast enhancement – a stone is noted in the common bile duct. Upon returning from the scanner, he is guarding his abdomen in agony.

Dustin is a 25-year-old White man who is presenting with two days of severe right knee pain. Dustin's pain began after sustaining a major collision with a goal post during a football drill and has progressed to the point that he is unable to bear weight on his right knee. On physical examination, you detect swelling of the right knee and significantly reduced range of motion secondary to severe pain. You obtain X-rays of the knee, which reveal comminuted intra-articular fractures. Knee MRI demonstrates disruption of multiple ligaments in the right knee. Dustin has been taking acetaminophen and ibuprofen for pain control, but has had minimal relief.

Shane is a 45-year-old White man who presents with new back pain after a fall from a ladder. The pain is focal in his lower back and does not radiate but has rapidly progressed in intensity in the few hours since the fall. Shane has full strength, sensation and normal rectal tone on physical exam. You note that his back is very tender to palpation at approximately T12-L1. You order a CT scan of the lumbar spine, which reveals a new chance fracture of the L1 vertebral body – both pedicles have been disrupted.

Douglas is a 50-year-old White man who presents after a motor vehicle collision. Douglas's car was struck from the passenger side and ultimately rolled over into a ditch. Douglas has sustained multiple superficial injuries and is in severe pain. Douglas endorses left sided chest pain when taking deep breaths as well as neck pain and diffuse body aches. Douglas undergoes a full trauma assessment with appropriate imaging studies. Except for two left rib fractures, he has no other radiographic evidence of acute injury, and no pneumothorax. Douglas is placed in a cervical collar, which helps with his neck pain, however his chest pain remains severe. Douglas's vital signs are stable, and his physical exam is remarkable for superficial abrasions, tenderness to palpation of his neck and left chest, but no other focal musculoskeletal injuries.

Patient B is a 35-year-old presenting to your emergency room after a bicycle accident. Patient B states they were biking down their usual mountain route when they lost control and skidded off the path. They fell off their bicycle, tumbling over some rocks and bushes. Patient B endorses multiple painful bruises on their arms and legs, and on physical exam you note that there are multiple ecchymoses and scrapes on both arms and shins that are tender to touch. However, Patient B can ambulate independently and has full range of motion in all joints. You complete a trauma survey and do not detect any open wounds or fractures. Patient B calmly asks if he can receive some pain medicine.

Bradley is an 86-year-old White man with history of multiple myeloma who presents with 6 months of progressive neck pain and limb weakness. Bradley states that his pain is triggered by flexion or extension of his neck. The pain has become severe and he is worried that it prevents his participation in daily activities. Bradley is also requiring more assistance to ambulate, citing that he is feeling weakness of his arms and legs. NSAIDs have not provided any pain relief. Through physical examination, you detect diffuse numbness and weakness in all his extremities. You also identify Hoffmann signs and hyperreflexia in both of his arms and legs. You obtain MRI and CT scans of his cervical spine, and discover a large tumor involving C4-C5 with epidural extension resulting in severe stenosis and kyphotic deformity. There are also innumerable osteolytic lesions throughout the visible spine segments.

Brett is a 77-year-old White man with history of lung cancer who presents with 3 months of diffuse back pain and progressive, unintentional weight loss. Brett describes the pain as constant and exacerbated by bending and twisting movements of his spine. In addition to increasing pain, he endorses progressive diffuse weakness, and he now to requires a front-wheel-walker to ambulate. Upon examining Brett, you find that he is cachetic and diffusely deconditioned. You palpate the full length of his spine and note that he is diffusely tender. You review the MRI of his full spine and identify innumerable lesions in all spine segments and multiple pathologic fractures.

Scott is a 65-year-old White man with 5 months of mid back pain. Scott states that the pain has gradually reached peak intensity and now interrupts his sleep. No medications have helped with his pain. When you perform a physical exam, you find that he has diminished sensation in his mid thoracic dermatomes, and his back is not tender to palpation. You also note that his eyes and mucous membranes were more pale than normal. Concerned for this constellation of signs/symptoms, you order for MRI of his thoracic spine, which reveals a large mass involving the gastric body and extending posteriorly into the spinal column. You also note multiple additional lesions in several distant regions of the thorax.

Kurt is a 59-year-old White man with neurofibromatosis with 8 months of progressive pain from thoracic spinal neurofibromas and a new diagnosis of glioblastoma after a recent seizure. Kurt explains that he previously has managed his pain with NSAIDs and neuropathic medications, however he noticed that it has progressed to the point that his regimen is no longer effective. When asked to describe the pain, he says that it is sharp and radiates from his back to his sternum. On your physical examination, you find that Kurt has no focal neurological deficits. You decide to obtain a thoracic MRI for surveillance of his neurofibromas, and find that they have increased in size.

Todd is a 75-year-old White man with history of lung cancer and 4 months of progressive low-back and right leg pain. Todd describes the pain as a dull ache that shoots down his right leg in no particular pattern or frequency. Recently, he started experiencing intermittent numbness throughout his right leg. Overall, he believes the pain is becoming more frequent and intolerable, as it now interrupts his sleep nightly and acetaminophen and ibuprofen have not helped. On your physical examination, you find that Todd has diffusely diminished sensation in his leg, but his strength and reflexes are normal. Upon reviewing his lumbar spine MRI, you identify diffuse leptomeningeal disease.

Chad is a 48-year-old White man with history of colorectal cancer that has progressed despite aggressive therapy. Chad began to experience diffuse back and pelvic pain 2 months ago but declined a visit to his oncologist. Instead, he tried to manage his pain with NSAIDs. Chad now presents to you with intolerable pain, and he says it has not responded to his efforts. On your. physical examination, you incidentally discover a left foot drop and diminished sensation in his left foot. MRI of his lumbar spine shows diffuse bony metastases, with a metastatic lesion involving the left L5-S1 neuroforamen.

Matthew is a 51-year-old White man with renal cell carcinoma status-post T4-T7 corpectomy and fusion for spine metastases 6 months ago who presents with progressive leg pain. Matthew states that the pain he had prior to his last surgery is returning and in a worse form. Specifically, he endorses that in addition to mid-back pain, he is experiencing shooting pains down both legs. The pain is worse with any ambulatory movement, and is not alleviated by ibuprofen or acetaminophen. When you examine Matthew, you identify tenderness to palpation of his lumbar spine and diminished sensation in his anterior thighs. You obtain MRI scans of his entire spine and discover that in addition to new metastatic lesions in the lumbar spine causing multilevel severe stenosis, there is evidence of adjacent level disease near his prior construct.

Dustin is a 29-year-old White man metastatic medulloblastoma status-post multiple rounds of chemotherapy and radiation therapy, presenting with several months of progressive leg pain. Dustin describes the pain as sometimes crampy and other times sharp, involving different regions of both his legs at different times. In addition to his deconditioning, he is now unable to sleep due to constant pain. On physical examination, you detect diffuse bilateral lower extremity weakness with intact sensation. You obtain a surveillance MRI of his entire spine and discover drop metastases seeding extensive regions of his spinal cord and thecal sac, with multiple lower nerve roots engorged by tumor.

Shane is a 38-year-old White man with a known cervical chordoma status-post multiple resections presenting with 2 months of progressive neck pain accompanied with thoracic and abdominal pain. Shane describes the pain as the worst it has ever been, as it feels like his neck, chest and abdomen are constantly on fire. Acetaminophen and ibuprofen provide no relief, and he is now unable to sleep. On physical exam, you note dysesthesia to palpation of his neck and pain to deep palpation of his abdomen. CT and MRI of his cervical spine, chest and abdomen reveal florid recurrence of disease with new lesions in his lungs and liver.

Douglas is a 45-year-old White man with hepatocellular carcinoma status-post C4-C5 corpectomy and fusion 8 months ago who presents with new arm and leg pain. Of note, Douglas endorses unintentional weight loss over the last 2 months which coincided with increased severity of his pain. When describing the pain, he says that he feels intermittent shocks down both arms and legs, and also notes a diffuse ache in his neck and lower back. Tylenol and ibuprofen have not been effective, and Douglas is due to revisit his oncologist since completing his last radiation treatment. Physical examination reveals some numbness in his hands and thighs, as well as diffuse spine tenderness. MRI of scans of his entire spine show increased tumor burden in his lumbar and cervical spine causing multiple areas of severe stenosis. You are also able to identify new lesions seeding his peritoneum.

Patient B is a 50 year old with bladder cancer status-post treatment with cisplatin chemotherapy. For several months, they have had progressive pain, numbness and paresthesias in both hands and feet. Patient B has tried ibuprofen with limited relief. On physical examination, you note that they have symmetrically diminished sensation in a stocking-glove distribution. You also note that they have difficulty maintaining balance and that they have a positive Romberg sign. Patient B recalls that their oncologist warned that cisplatin could cause neuropathy, but had hoped it would improve over time. Patient B would like help with managing their pain.

Bradley is a 52-year-old White man who presents to your clinic with complaints of low back and leg pain. Bradley’s pain started gradually several years ago, and he state that the pain has been more severe for several months. Bradley says that ibuprofen and other over the counter pain medicines have not helped. Bradley has also tried physical therapy. Bradley’s physical exam is remarkable for pain limitation of the bilateral lower extremities.  Bradley was recently diagnosed with moderate-severe lumbar spondylosis by a neurosurgeon, and was told that he would eventually require a spinal fusion. Bradley is considering surgery but he would like for the pain to be well controlled until he reaches a decision.

Brett is a 75-year-old White man who presents to your primary care clinic with progressive neck and arm pain. The pain started 2 months ago and is primarily axial and exacerbated with neck movement. Brett denies any numbness or weakness, but has had difficulty with his balance and hand dexterity along with shooting pains down his arms. Brett otherwise has been in generally good health, and reports that he has a high tolerance for pain but has tried over the counter medication and physical therapy with no relief. Brett's physical exam is remarkable for pain limited range of motion on flexion and extension of his cervical spine, positive Romberg sign, and bilateral Hoffman signs. Your initial workup reveals severe cervical spondylosis with canal stenosis.  Brett has never been in this much pain and is wondering what you can offer to relieve it.

Scott is a 42-year-old White man who comes to your office with a 2-year history of severe pain in his right lower back, right buttock, and posterior thigh. Scott endorses a history of prior back injury and had a fall preceding his current pain. Scott does physical therapy reports only taking ibuprofen for the pain with minimal relief. On physical exam, you confirm that he has pain-limited range of motion on right hip flexion and identify right paraspinal muscle tenderness to palpation. On passive straight leg raising, his pain is exacerbated. The rest of his physical exam is otherwise unremarkable. MRI of his lumbar spine confirms a disc herniation at L4-5.

Kurt is a 66-year-old White man who presents with 3 months of low-back pain. The pain is primarily axial and is exacerbated by bending, twisting and heavy lifting. Kurt has tried managing this pain with NSAIDs and low impact exercises recommended by a physical therapist, but his pain continues to worsen. On physical exam, his lumbar spine is tender to palpation, but he has no focal neurologic deficits. On further questioning, he reveals that he has had intermittent fevers and night sweats ever since he was hospitalized for a kidney infection 5 months ago. You obtain an MRI with contrast of his lumbar spine which reveals L3-4 pathology consistent with discitis-osteomyelitis and psoas abscesses.

Todd is a 38-year-old White man who presents with 6 months of shoulder pain and progressive hand weakness. Todd reports that his pain started after a car accident, and has not improved despite trying ibuprofen, acetaminophen and physical therapy. A steroid injection did relieve some of the pain, but he says this was short-lived and he feels that he is reaching a breaking point with the pain. During your physical exam, you note that he has some weakness on shoulder abduction and bilateral Hoffman's signs. Todd reveals that he was seen by a neurosurgeon two months ago, who informed Todd that his MRI showed a herniated disk at C4-5 causing neuroforaminal and canal stenosis. The neurosurgeon advised that Todd would need an anterior spine surgery, but Todd declined at that time. Repeat CT and MRi of the cervical spine confirm a disc herniation at C4-5 with slight progression in the canal stenosis.

Chad is a 44-year-old White man who presents with 2 months of low-back and leg pain. The pain started after a day of heavy yard work and has progressed gradually over time. Chad describes the pain as a dull ache in his lower back that is accompanied by intense shooting pains down his leg to the sole of his left foot. In the last three weeks, he endorses tripping and stumbling more frequently, and has been told by friends that he is dragging his left foot. At present time he is most concerned about the increasing severity of pain, which is affecting his ability to function. When you examine Chad, you confirm that he has a left foot drop with diminished sensation in the sole of his foot. You order an MRI, which reveals an L5-S1 disc herniation with associated canal stenosis and left neuroforaminal stenosis.

Matthew is a 53-year-old White man who presents with 6 months of neck and arm pain with progressive gait difficulties. Matthew reports that he was in a car accident 6 months ago where he sustained some neck trauma, but he chose to leave the hospital against medical advice. Since then, he has had progressive neck pain with intermittent electrical-type pains involving his arms and sometimes his legs. Matthew also describes significant difficulty with balance and gait, for which he now uses a wheelchair to avoid falling. On physical exam, you identify brisk reflexes in his upper and lower extremities, poor proprioception, and weakness throughout both upper extremities. MRI of the cervical spine shows a type-2 fracture of the odontoid process of C2, with a fracture fragment angulated toward the spinal cord causing severe stenosis and cord signal change.

Dustin is a 60-year-old White man with history of prior L5-S1 posterior lumbar fusion who presents with 8 months of new thigh pain. Dustin states that he was previously in good health and pain-free since his last surgery, but for the last 8 months, he has had progressive discomfort in his anterior thighs. This discomfort has transformed into severe pain in the last 3 months, which he says is worse after prolonged ambulation and often keeps his from sleeping. When you examine Dustin, you discover bilateral hip flexor weakness and diminished sensation over his anterior thighs and knees. MRI and CT of the lumbar spine show intact instrumentation at L5-S1, but with new degenerative changes at L4-L5 resulting in canal and neuroforaminal stenosis. The findings are consistent with adjacent-level disease.

Shane is a 57-year-old White man with history of prior C3-C6 posterior cervical fusion presenting with 4 months of new neck, hand and arm pain. Shane was doing well for several years after his last surgery, but he now reports severe pain in his from his 3rd-5th digits and the medial aspect of his arms. Your physical examination confirms diminished sensation in this distribution, and you also detect weakness of his hand intrinsic muscles. CT and MRI of the cervical spine who intact instrumentation at C3-C6, but with new degenerative changes spanning C6-T1 resulting in canal and neuroforaminal stenosis - consistent with adjacent-level disease.

Douglas is a 55-year-old White man presenting with 9 months of progressive low-back and leg pain. Douglas states that his pain is worse after prolonged ambulation and radiates to his right buttock and thigh. The pain has become constant in the last 2 months and he is unable to function effectively at his job because of the pain. Douglas has tried physical therapy and conservative pain medications including epidural steroid injections and NSAIDs. On physical exam, you observe that his pain is significantly worse with a right straight-leg raise and there are no focal deficits. MRI of the lumbar spine reveals grade-2 spondylolisthesis at L4-L5 with degenerative changes contributing to severe canal and neuroforaminal stenosis. Flexion-extension X rays show dynamic instability of L4 on L5.

Patient B is a 62-year-old who presents to your clinic with joint pains. Patient B says their pain is worst in both knees and has persisted for six months. Patient B endorses pain relief with ibuprofen. Patient B has not tried physical therapy. There are no motor deficits on physical exam, and their knees appear slightly swollen but with full range of motion. X-rays of their knees show findings consistent with osteoarthritis. Patient B is wondering about their options for pain control.

Bradley is a 62-year-old White man who is post-op day 3 status-post bi-frontal craniotomy for resection of an olfactory groove meningioma. Surgery was uncomplicated, and he has been healing well with no new deficits beyond expected loss of smell. Bradley is meeting all milestones for discharge, however he continues to have significant head pain at the site of his craniotomy. During your pre-discharge physical examination, you note that there is expected frontal scalp swelling and tenderness to palpation of his incision site. You review the medication administration record and see that he has required 1 dose of hydrocodone every 6 hours for pain control.

Brett is a 35-year-old White man who is post-op day 2 status-post left pterional craniotomy for clipping of an unruptured aneurysm. Surgery was uncomplicated and he is on track to be discharged today. Brett only complains of persistent head pain at the surgical site. During your physical examination, you find expected post-operative swelling and tenderness of his left scalp tissues. The medical administration record shows that he has been needing 1 dose of hydrocodone every 6 hours for pain control.

Scott is a 55-year-old White man who is post-op day 4 status-post C3-C5 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion. Scott had some difficulty swallowing on post op day 1 which has improved and he is now able to take solid medications. In addition, he states that his arm pains have improved, but he continues to have significant surgical site pain and residual arm pain not relieved by acetaminophen. On physical examination, you find that his neck remains tender to palpation and he continues to have dysesthesias in both arms. The medication administration record indicates that he has been taking 1 dose of oxycodone every 6 hours for pain control.

Kurt is a 63-year-old White man who is post-op day 5 status-post C3-T1 posterior cervical decompression and fusion for cervical myelopathy. Kurt's post-operative recovery has been smooth and he is to be discharged later today, however he is having pain at his surgical site. Physical examination is remarkable for improving bilateral upper extremity strength, sensation and gait, and you confirm that he is very tender at their surgical site. Per the medication administration record, he has needed 1 dose of oxycodone every 4 hours, along with acetaminophen and cyclobenzaprine.

Todd is a 52-year-old White man who is post-op day 4 status-post L3-L4 laminectomy for lumbar stenosis. Surgery was uncomplicated, and he has met goals for discharge. Todd endorses resolution of his leg pains but continues to have severe pain at his surgical site. On physical examination, you confirm that he is neurologically intact and has expected tenderness to palpation of his lower back at the surgical site. Per the medication administration record, in addition to cyclobenzaprine and acetaminophen, Todd has been needing oxycodone every 6 hours for pain control.

Chad is a 57-year-old White man who is post-op day 5 status-post L4-L5 transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion for severe back and leg pain. There were no surgical complications, and he continues to have low back and leg pain though he endorses steady improvement in his symptoms. When you examine Chad, you confirm that he has no new neurological deficits, and does have persistent pain at his lumbar surgical site. Upon checking the medication administration record, you note that he has required acetaminophen and oxycodone every 6 hours for pain control.

Matthew is a 32-year-old White man who is post-op day 3 status-post endoscopic endonasal approach for transsphenoidal resection of a pituitary adenoma. Matthew's hospital stay was uncomplicated, and today he only complains of head pain. During your daily physical assessment, you find that he is neurologically intact and that he has expected amounts of sanguinous discharge from his nares. The medication administration record shows that he has needed 1 dose of hydrocodone every 8 hours for pain control.

Dustin is a 25-year-old White man who is post-op day 4 status-post suboccipital craniectomy for Chiari type-1 malformation. The surgery was uncomplicated, however Dustin experienced severe nausea and vomiting for 2 days after surgery. Dustin now feels better, and he says that his headaches have improved, but he is having a lot of pain at his suboccipital incision site. On physical examination, he has no neurological deficits, and his surgical site and posterior neck are tender to palpation. A post-operative MRI confirms adequate decompression of his Chiari malformation and no hydrocephalus. Per the medication administration record, he has required some hydrocodone every 8 hours for pain control.

Shane is a 39-year-old White man who is post-op day 2 status-post right retromastoid craniotomy with retrosigmoid approach and microvascular decompression for trigeminal neuralgia. Shane has had complete resolution of his trigeminal neuralgia and meets discharge criteria, but remarks that pain at the surgical site is his primary concern. During physical examination, you find that he is neurologically intact and note that there is incisional swelling and tenderness to palpation. Passive and active neck rotation exacerbates his pain. The medication administration record indicates that he is needing hydrocodone every 6 hours for pain control.

Douglas is a 45-year-old White man who is post-op day 16 status post left craniotomy for clipping of a ruptured aneurysm. Douglas's post operative course has been very smooth, and he has had no episodes of clinical vasospasm. After removing his external ventricular drain, you examine Douglas and find that [subjective] is neurologically intact. Douglas's head CT today shows some residual blood products in the subarachnoid space and at the surgical site, but no concerning radiographic findings. As you prepare to discharge Douglas in the coming days, you examine the medication administration record and note that he has required hydrocodone every 8 hours for headache management.

Patient B is a 46-year-old who is now one week status-post left carpal tunnel release surgery. Pre-operatively, they were having numbness and pain in their left digits 1-3 for several months.
